opus-5.5.text:
I think of it less as a jump and more as a gradual pull toward the parts of the problem that felt most unresolved to me.

When I started in theoretical machine learning, I was drawn to questions like: why does learning work at all, what are the right abstractions, and what guarantees can we actually prove? That training was really valuable. It gave me a habit of asking what the core difficulty of a problem is, instead of just trying things until something works.

Over time, though, I noticed that many of the assumptions that make theory clean, like i.i.d. data, a fixed distribution, and a well-specified objective, are exactly what break down when an agent acts in the world. The moment your decisions change the data you see next, you're in sequential decision-making territory, and that's where imitation learning and reinforcement learning become natural. Imitation learning was an interesting bridge for me because it has a very crisp theoretical story, things like compounding errors and distribution shift between the expert's states and the learner's states, and yet it's also one of the most practical ways to get robots to do useful things today.

Then moving onto real hardware was, honestly, a humbling experience. On a real robot you can't hide behind a simulator or an idealized model. Sensors are noisy, contacts are messy, data is expensive, and every failure costs time and sometimes broken parts. But that's also what makes it exciting. You get very direct feedback about whether your ideas actually matter.

So the way I see it, theory taught me how to think carefully, imitation learning gave me a framework that connects that thinking to practice, and robotics forces honesty. I still find myself going back and forth: an observation on the robot raises a question, and sometimes the cleanest way to understand it is to step back and formalize it. I think that loop between principled understanding and physical reality is where a lot of progress in robot learning is going to come from.

r001.rationale: The response mentions noisy sensors, messy contacts, and costly failures on real hardware, but it does not compare the precision required for robot manipulation with that of typical machine-learning tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, it didn't feel like a straight line at the time. When I was doing theory, I spent most of my days thinking about sample complexity, generalization bounds, convergence rates. Clean problems, clean assumptions. And I loved that. But at some point I noticed that the assumptions I was most comfortable with were exactly the ones that break the moment you touch a physical system.

So the shift came from a kind of discomfort. I had all these results about what a learner should be able to do, and I had no idea whether any of it mattered when the data comes from a noisy camera and a gripper that slips. Imitation learning was the natural bridge. It's close enough to supervised learning that my theory instincts still applied. You have demonstrations, you fit a policy, you can reason about distribution shift and compounding errors. That's a problem theorists had already named. But on hardware, you feel it. You watch a robot drift three centimeters off its training distribution and then do something completely absurd, and suddenly the abstract notion of covariate shift has a very concrete smell of burnt motors.

Reinforcement learning was the next step because imitation alone caps you at whatever the demonstrator did. The robot can't get better than the human, and humans are slow and inconsistent and tired at four in the afternoon. RL gives you a way to improve from the robot's own experience. But real-world RL is brutal. You don't get millions of free samples. Every episode costs time, every reset might need a person, and a bad exploratory action can break something expensive. So a lot of my recent work is really about being frugal: how do you use a small number of demonstrations to shape exploration, how do you make the reward signal cheap enough to actually collect, how do you fine-tune without forgetting the safe behaviors you started with.

What I'd say about the progression overall is that the theory never went away. It changed its job. In the beginning, theory was the product. Now it's more like a compass. It tells me which failures are fundamental and which are engineering. When something doesn't work on the robot, the first question I ask is whether this is a problem that no amount of data would fix, or just a problem of not enough data, bad representation, poor action parameterization. Having that lens saves a lot of wasted weeks.

And I think the direction of influence is starting to reverse, too. The things that break on hardware are pointing toward theory questions that I don't think the field has really answered yet. Why does fine-tuning a pretrained visuomotor policy with a few hundred real trials sometimes work beautifully and sometimes collapse? That's not an engineering question. That's a question about what the pretraining actually learned and what structure the small-data regime is exploiting. So in a strange way, going to the robot made me a better theorist, because now I know which questions are worth asking.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes hardware sensitivity, including a robot drifting three centimeters, but does not state that manipulation requires substantially greater precision than typical machine-learning tasks.

astra-6.text:
I see it as a progression toward asking what it takes for learning to actually produce useful behavior. In theoretical machine learning, you can isolate a question and study it under clear assumptions. With robotics, those assumptions become things you have to confront: what can the robot observe, how good is the data, and what happens when its actions take it somewhere the training data didn’t cover?

That’s where imitation learning and reinforcement learning fit together for me. Demonstrations give the robot a starting point—a way to learn useful behavior without discovering everything through trial and error. But imitation alone raises the question of recovery: if the robot makes a small mistake, can it get back on track? Reinforcement learning offers a way to improve through interaction, although on real hardware you have to care about the cost and safety of every attempt.

So I don’t see it as leaving theory behind. It’s more about letting the physical system sharpen the questions. You still want to understand why a method works, but you also need to know whether it works reliably when the robot actually touches something.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as a progression from asking what makes learning work in principle to asking what it takes to make learning work in the physical world. In theoretical machine learning, you try to isolate a problem and understand the assumptions behind a result. With a real robot, those assumptions become very concrete: What can the robot observe? Where does the training data come from? What happens when it encounters something outside that data?

That’s where imitation learning and reinforcement learning become complementary. Demonstrations can give the robot a useful starting point, especially when discovering a behavior through trial and error would be expensive. Reinforcement learning offers a way to improve through interaction, including learning how to recover when things go wrong.

So I don’t see theory and hardware as separate directions. Theory gives you a way to reason about a problem, and hardware pushes you to ask whether you’re reasoning about the right problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the challenges of applying learning on physical robots, but does not say that robot manipulation required substantially greater precision than typical machine-learning tasks.
